Far-right rhetoric that authorizes is not a side effect of this trend. It's one of its drivers. Deliberate desecrations of holy Quran, attacks on mosques, and the stigmatization of Muslim communities are not isolated provocations. Hatred, once normalized, does not remain rhetorical. It translates into fear, violence, and fractured communities. Our citizens abroad experience this reality every day, from the housing market to the schoolyard. Freedom of expression is not a license for hatred. International law is clear on this, and this Council has shown the way through resolutions 16, 18, and 53.1. What is missing is not standards, but political will to apply them fully and to everyone. That includes those most inclined to lecture others. In Iceland, it's reported that authorities have been urged to confront hate speech against migrants, especially online, amid a persistent failure even to record such cases. The digital space has become the newest frontier of this struggle. Algorithms amplify what device and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, must not become new vectors of hate. Turkey will continue to combat racism, xenophobia, anti-Muslim racism, and anti-immigrant hatred in all their forms, and to play its part in this Council's efforts to that end. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I now recognise the distinguished representative of Sudan.

Thank you very much, Vice-President. We have taken due note of the relevant reports providing updates concerning racism, racial discrimination and associated intolerance. We align ourselves with the recommendations made in those reports, suggesting that we must incorporate combating racial discrimination in school curricula. We must also ensure schooling that is free of charge in the poorest regions and countries, and support efforts being made by the committee to ensure the universal ratification of the CERD. We also recognize the work of the expert group and its report. Slavery and racism, as well as intolerance and violence, tend to target the most vulnerable groups, migrants, victims of conflicts, and minorities in general, and that is why the war that is being waged in Sudan opens the door to different avenues of discrimination against communities. Verbal violence, physical violence in Darfur and other Sudanese regions bear witness to this. Human rights reports document these violations and crimes, and we therefore call on all countries to support us in combating the militia supporting racism in Sudan and others.
Nigeria has the floor.

Mr. Vice President, Nigeria aligns with the African Group and affirm its unequivocal condemnation of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. Nigeria takes note of the report of the other committee on the elaboration of complementary standards and welcomes its collaboration to address gaps in protection against contemporary manifestation of racism as xenophobia. Mr. Vice President, as we commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Program of Action, it's relevant to remain undeniably across regions, Africa and people of African descent continue to face racial profiling, hate speech, discrimination, and xenophobic violence. Migrants are increasingly portrayed as threats and blamed for economic and social difficulties, creating conditions that normalize exclusion and violence. Nigeria is also concerned about the potential for artificial intelligence to reinforce existing bias and further exacerbate racial discrimination. This development and use must therefore be transparent, accountable, and supported by appropriate safeguards. Finally, Nigeria underscores the importance of international cooperation and reparative justice to address both present discrimination and the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism. I thank you.
Thank you very much. I now recognize the distinguished representation of Tunisia. They appear not to be present. And so I now recognize the distinguished representative of Ukraine.

Mr. President, Ukraine reaffirms its commitment to combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related forms of intolerance in all their manifestations. Against this background, we remain deeply concerned by Russia's systematic discriminatory policies in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. Ukrainians face persecution and oppression on the grounds of their national or ethnic origin, identity, and language. This practice is from part to Russia's broader policy aimed at suppressing Ukrainian identity and erasing its presence in the occupied territories. Indigenous people of Ukraine, in particular Crimean Tatars, continue to face targeted repressions, restrictions on their cultural and religious rights, and persecution for opposing Russia's occupation.

These policies.

Are enforced by Russian state-sponsored propaganda and rhetoric that deny the existence of distinct Ukrainian identity and fuel hatred and intolerance against Ukrainians. Russia also exert systematic pressure on residents of the occupied territories to acquire Russian citizenship. Those who refuse face intimidation, restriction on access to essential services, and the risk of detention. At the same time, Russia seeks to alter the demographic composition of the occupied territories through the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainians, while facilitating the relocation of Russian citizens there. Ukraine calls upon the international community to firmly oppose such discriminatory policies, combat hatred and intolerance, and ensure accountability.

For violations.
Thank you very much. I now recognize the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania.

Thank you, Mr. Vice-President. Tanzania aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group. We welcome the report of the Group of Independent Eminent Experts and reaffirm our commitment to combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. 25 years after its adoption, full implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action remains essential. We must address contemporary manifestations of racism and other historical roots, including slavery, colonialism, and other forms of exploitation. We are concerned by racism and hate speech in digital spaces. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, must uphold equality and human dignity and avoid reinforcing discrimination. Education, in particular for young people, is vital to promote tolerance, mutual respect, and peaceful coexistence. We call for stronger international cooperation, capacity building, and constructive dialogue to support implementation, taking account of national circumstances and the developing countries' priorities. Tanzania remains committed to working with all member states toward a world free from racism and discrimination. I thank you, Mr. Vice President.
Thank you very much. And I recognize the distinguished representative of Uganda.

Mr. President, we align with the statements of NAM, the African group, and OIC groups. Racism has no place in any modern society and should not have the slightest nuance in any society, including in the UN with over two decades of the DDPA. My government, Uganda, is renowned for its principled position against all forms of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and any kind of related intolerance. Full eradication of racial discrimination starts with the political will, coupled with international implementation of the law and sensitization of the populace. We therefore call on our system member states to transparently address the underlying causes of discrimination by intentionally and willingfully reviewing national policies and legal systems that enable and entrench systematic racial discrimination against persons of especially African descent. Mr. President, racism is an affront to human dignity and equality and should be condemned. Racism has been entrenched in systems and structures that largely black people, especially people of African descent, is a shame and a testament to not only double standards in the approach of human rights, but also manifestation of a serious superiority complex. My government remains committed to fight against all forms of discrimination, including implementation of the tenants of the Durban Declaration. I thank you.

Thank you very much. And I recognize the distinguished representative of Togo. They appear not to be in the room. Okay, so that was the last speaker on my list. We'll now move on to the list of speakers from national human rights institutions and non-governmental organizations. I therefore pass the floor to Jerusalem Institute of Justice.

Mr. President, my name is Eli Sharabi, I'm survivor of torture. On October 7, Hamas terrorists kidnapped me from my home and murdered my wife, Lian, and my daughters, Noa and Yehel. My brother, Yossi, was killed after more than 100 days in captivity, where he was used as a human shield. For 491 days, I was held underground, chained, starved, beaten, and humiliated. I learned my family was dead only upon my release. I'm here to call on you to use your mandate to bring change. The Jerusalem Institute of Justice documented the deliberate starvation of over 78 hostages, on return weighing just 44 kilos. October 7 Justice Without Borders documented patterns of physical and psychological torture affecting 255 hostages and their families, some for over two years and even a decade. I've chosen the road of justice beyond politics and grounded in our shared humanity. This council must act, recognize the torture, demand criminal investigations, and confront the terrorist networks. Name these crimes and impunity.
Muchas gracias. Thank you very much. I recognize the International Association of Jewish Lawyers and Tourists.

25 years after Durban, this anniversary should be an opportunity not only to ask whether the Durban framework has been fully implemented, but also to examine how its language has been involved in practice. The independent eminent expert rightly warned that political narratives, misinformation and stigmatization can transform minorities into perceived threats. normalize hatred and ultimately contribute to violence. Yet the report does not examine whether the language of anti-racism and human rights can itself be politicized. As IJEL documented in our submission to this Council over the past 25 years, language originally intended to combat racism has increasingly been instrumentalized to portray Israel as uniquely illegitimate. It is this language that has helped turn what should be legitimate criticism of policies into collective blame, exclusion, and intimidation of Jews, worldwide. What we have witnessed over the past 25 years should serve as a warning to everyone who cares about human rights. Political actors, organizations, and in some cases states, have sought to use the language of Durban to cloak anti-Semitic narratives into the language of anti-racism and human rights in schools, universities, across social medias, and within this institution. We therefore urge the UN to critically reassess the Durban framework, recognize contemporary anti-Semitism in all its forms, and apply the IRM working definition as part of its efforts to eliminate all forms of racism.

Thank you.

Thank you very much. I recognize Bedna Barys.

Mr. President, on December 14, my family was evacuated from a Jewish festival as gunfire erupted nearby at Bondi Beach in Australia. Since then, I've recorded for posterity the stories of the 15 killed and the 42 shot in a documentary and book. Among them, 10-year-old Matilda, whose parents had brought her to Bondi for face painting and bubbles. She was gunned down and the doctors couldn't save her. Holocaust survivor Alex Clayman was also killed, as was Rabbi Eli Schlanger and Edith Bruckman. A newborn baby hospitalized with shrapnel wounds, while a couple in their 60s, Boris and Sophia German, sacrificed their lives confronting the shooters. According to court documents, the attackers had condemned the actions of Zionists. This shows, clear as night follows day, that hatred against Zionists leads to violence against Jews. Anti-Zionism is inextricably linked to anti-Semitism. Across the diaspora, this movement has proved violent and deadly. I implore the Human Rights Council to wake up to what's happening to Jews around the world and take action against this hate before more innocent lives are lost. Thank you.
Thank you very much. And I recognize the Arab Organization Against Torture and Enforced Disappearance.

We address the Arab Council. especially related to ethnic, racial, sectarian discrimination practiced by the Houthi militia in Yemen. The Houthi militia in Yemen is based on exclusionary ideology rooted in the claim of a divine right, viewing Yemenis merely as subjects and slaves. Since Yemen's catastrophe in September 2014, the Houthis have dismantled state institutions and killed more than half a million Yemenis. They have abducted academics, politicians, activists, journalists, and even UN personnel that are imprisoned in Sana'a. Here I stand before you in a wheelchair where I have been confined for the past 12 years as a result of an objection to torture in Houthi detention facilities, a consequence of racial discrimination. This conversation is in a systematic work against future generations. The Houthis are targeting approximately 1.6 million students in the areas under their control. This year, Houthi summer sent-- targeted approximately 461,000 students with the aim of turning them into fighters indoctrinated into sectarian ideology, input from Iran and Iraq, and drawing them to invade Yemeni cities. In the face of this humanitarian catastrophe, where is the free world? In the face of the most egregious forms of racial discrimination, we call upon the System Council to condemn these practices and hold responsible to account, put an end to the systemic destruction of Yemeni society. We call for international actions to put an end to this situation. It is necessary to stop the destruction of cities and families.
I give the floor to the Sikh Human Rights Group.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. 25 years after the Durban Declaration, racism, racial discrimination and xenophobia remain persistent in many societies. Legal protections and accountability remain essential. However, the continued presence of prejudice also shows the limits of addressing discrimination only after it has occurred. We therefore welcome the attention this session gives to education as a tool to prevent racism. Education should not only teach what discrimination is prohibited. It should also help societies become comfortable with difference and recognise diversity as a normal and enriching part of human life. As the Council also considers complementary standards, we believe these should address not only gaps in law but also gaps in prevention. The Sikh Human Rights Group has therefore proposed a non-binding declaration on diversity, encouraging states to develop positive programs in education, institutions and community life that promote interaction, understanding and acceptance. Such a declaration would not replace the Durban framework or existing protections. It would complement them by addressing the attitudes and fears from which discrimination often grows. Preventing racism requires not only stronger laws, but societies resilient to prejudice and division. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to International Youth and Student Movement for the United Nations.

Mr. President, We fully support the General Assembly adopted theme for the 25th anniversary as it was proposed by the Human Rights Council, mobilizing global public support for the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. It sends a clear message that the DDPA remains the cornerstone for our common work against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, and that its full and effective implementation is a global priority. Regrettably, the OHCHR has done little to promote the DDP at its 25th anniversary. but the commemoration of the DDPA 25th anniversary is for the full year. Therefore, we call on the OHCHR to fully implement the adopted General Assembly and Human Rights Council resolutions for a global outreach program in support of the DDPA, including publishing the DDPA for wide dissemination. Thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you. I give the floor to Center for Human Rights and Peace Advocacy.

Mr. Vice President, Center for Human Rights and Peace Advocacy draws the urgent attention of this Council to the systemic escalation of human rights violations inside Pakistan, including Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, PoK. There is a widening crackdown on basic freedoms, In PoK and Gilgit-Baltistan, peaceful public assemblies protesting economic marginalization have been met with arbitrary detentions, internet blockades, and excessive force by state security apparatuses. Several peaceful protesters, reportedly over 100, have lost their lives. Beyond these territories, ethnic and religious minorities in Balochistan, Sindh, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa face ongoing structural discrimination, arbitrary arrests, and unresolved cases of enforced disappearances. A state cannot demand international accountability while shielding its own systemic domestic abuses from oversight. We demand an immediate halt to the targeting of civil society, journalists and peaceful protesters in PoK in Pakistan. Call on Pakistan to allow independent UN fact-finding missions unhindered access to inspect these areas. Thank you, Mr. Vice.
President. Thank you very much. I give the floor to Centre Zargos pour les Droits de l'Homme. They're not in the room. I give the floor to United Nations Watch.

Mr. President, let's talk about racism in the Middle East. I grew up in Yemen, where the word that we used for black people is "abid," which quite literally means "slaves." Racism towards black people in my country is horrifying, but it's not even the most toxic hatred that I was taught. The first time I ever heard the word "Jew" was in my local mosque when I was nine years old. At the end of Friday prayers, the imam said, "May Allah kill the Jews and the Zionists." And I responded, alongside thousands of Muslims praying beside me, "Amin." I was taught that Zionism meant killing Arabs, stealing our land, and destroying Islam. Then October 7th came. Hamas terrorists freed Palestine by slaughtering 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping more than 200 people, including a one-year-old child. Almost everyone in my Arab Muslim circle celebrated. I didn't. Instead, as a journalist, I decided to visit the so-called Zionist entity. And I was completely shocked to the core by the lack of apartheid and racism that I experienced. One day I got an eye infection. At the hospital, the nurses in reception were Jewish. The doctor treating me was Arab. Is there racism in Israel? Of course. There's racism everywhere. But Arabs in Israel aren't called slaves. They're doctors, engineers, and party leaders. My experience helped me realize that Zionism really just means the Jewish people's right to a tiny country. Everything I was taught was a lie.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the Coordinating Board of Jewish Organizations.

Mr. President, the synagogue I serve as rabbi, Kehila Charit Torah of Toronto, was founded a half century ago by Canadian Jews and Jews from South Africa who left their native countries' turmoil under apartheid. These founders only sought a peaceful place to worship, raise their families, and celebrate life.

They enjoyed living out this hope until Hamas' October 7th attacks.

Some now take the Palestinian-Israeli conflict as license to attack Jews, harass Jews, and threaten Jews even thousands of miles distant from that conflict. Since 2023, our synagogue has been attacked more than 10 times, windows shattered, doors smashed, signs set on fire.

We are among Jewish institutions nationwide in Canada that have been harassed, shot at, and set aflame.

No Jewish citizen has felt completely safe.

Despite the best efforts of Toronto police, violence continues.

Last week, an assailant fired shots at a rural synagogue on a major holiday, and the world remains silent.

Elie Wiesel said, "It often begins with the Jews, and it almost never ends with the Jews.".

Darker days are ahead for our society unless we call out Jew hatred in Israel and abroad and cease tolerance and justification for these acts.

May God Almighty bless all our efforts to spread peace.

Thank you.

Thank you. I give the floor to Alak Haklo in the service of man.

Mr. Vice President, Israel's ongoing genocide, annexation, and unlawful occupation of Palestine cannot be separated from the racialized structures that dehumanize Palestinians, systematically deny their rights, and entrench apartheid on both sides of the green line. Across political, academic, and media discourse, Palestinian lives are rendered conditional. Their deaths are presented as statistics, while their immense suffering and destruction is either minimized or made invisible, despite this being the first livestream genocide. Genocidal violence against Palestinian men, women, and children is detached from the colonial context in which it occurs, while Palestinian resistance to grave violations of the most fundamental human rights is presented as criminal. The level of dehumanization of the Palestinian people and lack of accountability for Israel's escalating crimes has created a reality in which a state that can pass death penalty legislations targeting the very group it intends to destroy without any meaningful diplomatic, financial, or political consequences. The complicity of Western global north states in Israel's ongoing Nakba and settler colonial apartheid system has entrenched this culture of impunity, setting a dangerous precedent. Continued failure to implement the ICJ's 2024 advisory opinion further reveals a blatant double standard, where international law is invoked as universal, yet because of latent institutional discrimination, it fails to protect the freedom, dignity, and life of Palestinians. It is therefore crucial to show that racist and discriminatory policies and practices, wherever they occur, will not be tolerated. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to a joint statement by the International Organization for the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination.

Thank you. We welcome the observations presented concerning the persistence of racial discrimination and xenophobia in migration governance. As highlighted in the discussion, the legacies of enslavement and colonialism, together with structural inequalities, continue to contribute to exclusion, poverty, and marginalization. At the same time, the absence of sufficient safe pathways exposes migrants and refugees to dangerous journeys and increased dependence on smugglers. We are concerned about the allegations of excessive abusive practices by security and border control authorities. International standards call for immigration policies to be implemented without discrimination on the basis of race, color, or ethnic origin. IFORD and Geneva International Center for Justice calls on states to ensure that immigration and border policies comply fully with international human rights obligations. Protection for women and girls of African descent should be strengthened, including accessible mechanisms for reporting and responding to sexual and gender-based violence. Finally, we urge states to move beyond commitments and ensure that anti-racism principles are effectively incorporated into migration governance at national, regional, and international levels. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to Interfaith International.

Interfaith International in over 30 years history has actively contributed to the campaign against racism. Our members in their personal lives are affiliated to several different religions and they do not discriminate racially, no doubt because of these religions.

A belief in a higher power is shared by the different religions and this brings our members together.

In common action on behalf of anti-racism.

Our president and secretary.

General participated in the World Conference Against Racism held at Durban in South Africa in 2001 and its follow-up conferences. Religion by its very essence should promote the common action of people of different races and religions. We shall continue to support all anti-racism activities inside and outside this council We support CERD's recent decision on racial discrimination against asylum seekers and refugees in South Africa. We progress in understanding the genetic and linguistic unity of human beings, discoveries which destroy old racial concepts. We shall use these new discoveries in promoting work within the Council. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
Thank you. I give the floor for a joint statement, Instituto Brasileiro de Direitos Humanos.

UNARC, the Peregum Institute, the Black Evangelical Movement, and the Brazilian Institute of Human Rights call this Council's attention to the persistence of racialized police violence in Brazil. In October 2025, a police operation in Pena and Alemao complexes resulted in more than 120 deaths, becoming the deadliest police operation in the history of Rio.

We question the security model that repetitively exposes predominantly black communities to a highly lethal police operation.

CERT has already raised concerns about the disproportionate impact of police violence on Afro-Brazilians.

Emmler has said that killings of Afro-Brazilians by law enforcement are generalized and carried out in a systemic way, which suggests a social cleansing process designed to exterminate sectors of society deemed dangerous or criminal.

As the elections in Brazil draw near, opinion polls suggest that violence is one of the public's main concerns. In response, the far right is proposing more intense repression and greater use of force as solutions. However, UN experts and civil society have shown that law enforcement agencies disproportionately target Afro-descendants. In this regard, we urge Brazil to give greater priority to a public security policy system that focuses on protection of life, and we call on this Council to demand non-discriminatory and intersectional public security policies in Brazil. The Black youth cannot continue paying with their lives for the failures of public security.

Thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you. I give the floor to African Center for Democracy and Human Rights.

Mr. President, when the world gathered in Durban in 2001, millions of victims of racism looked at that occasion with great expectations. While these victims were yearning to dignity and an end to everyday discrimination, they were cherishing peaceful coexistence between members of our human race. 25 years after that solemn moment and momentum, the world ended up by realizing none of those valid aspirations. There is no peace in the world with all these inequalities, violation of international norms, and deadly intra- and interstate armed conflicts. What is especially disturbing is that racism and xenophobic sentiments are growing in a dangerous way in developed and developing countries. In Libya, as I speak now, hundreds of refugees from African countries are being aggressively attacked and chased away from their homes. We see xenophobia growing with the gains of extreme right-wing policies in the heart of Western European democracies. And we have seen discrimination in Asia during the COVID-19 epidemic when people of African descent were denied access to shopping centers because of the color of their skins. Mr. President, the Permanent Forum on People of African Descent, as a mechanism that defines the narrative of victims of racist phenomena and advises the Council on measures to address them, its independence and support of its work must therefore be fully guaranteed, especially in propagating the objectives and outcomes of the Durban Conference. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to Fundacion Vida, Grupo Ecolandico Verde.

Thank you, Mr. President. The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action commits states to equality and equal treatment before tribunals. I speak today as the daughter of Idris Khattak, a well-known Pashtun human rights defender from Pakistan. On 13 November 2019, my father was abducted from his car and disappeared. For seven months, our family did not know where he was or whether he was alive. In November 2021, a secret military court sentenced him to 14 years in prison following a secret trial. On 10th November 2025, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found his detention arbitrary and in violation of international law, and called for his immediate release, compensation, and an investigation. My father is 63. He is not allowed to make telephone calls and is not receiving much needed medical attention. In April 2026, UN experts warned that his uncontrolled diabetes and other medical conditions had become life-threatening and called for his immediate release. We call on this Council to urge Pakistan to release my father immediately and comply with the Durban Declaration and the Working Group's opinion. Thank you.

Thank you. I give the floor to International Federation for the Protection of the Rights of Ethnic, Religious, Linguistic and Other Minorities. Absent. I give the floor Centre du Commerce International pour le Developpement.

Thank you very much, President. Since the adoption of the Declaration of Durban and Programme of Action, many states have adopted national policies to combat racism, and the results achieved are still weak. The root causes of racism are known to all, and they are always the same victims, especially the poor, ethnic and religious minorities, indigenous peoples, people of African descent, migrants and refugees. CCSD commends the work of the CERD and strongly supports the development of complementary standards. During its 111th session, The third major recommendations on the current situation in South Africa, CCID calls upon South Africa to take adequate measures to protect migrants and put an end to xenophobic violence in the country. These violations must stop. Those responsible must be identified, impartially investigated and prosecuted, tried and where held responsible, convicted in accordance with the law. We also call on states to effectively implement the international instruments against racism on their territory, the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the DDPA. No economic hardship can justify racism. No migration policies justify hatred. Equality cannot remain a proclaimed principle. It should become effective protection to ensure that every human being, including those whom the majority considers to be foreign, thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to Association Caritative et du Temps pour la Jeunesse. They're not in the room. I give to the Association de Defense et Promotion des Droits de l'Homme.

Thank you, President. This month, Eelam Tamils around the world mourn Thiyathibam Thiliben, who gave his life in 1987 through a fast unto death, demanding justice and our people's right to self-determination. His sacrifice remains a timeless symbol of peaceful resistance. Yet even in mourning, we remain victims of Sri Lankan military occupation. Last Monday, his statue was removed. Erasing a memorial is not a neutral act. It attempts to erase the people's memory, identity, and history. This is racial discrimination in its structural form, a Sri Lankan state that suppresses Tamil remembrance while its army occupies our homeland in the North and East. It contradicts the Durban commitments to eliminate racism and to respect the identity and culture of peoples. President, Sri Lanka has reached the 10th stage of genocide, denial. Denial of Mullivaikail, denial of enforced disappearances, denial of mass graves. and now a denial of our right even to mourn. A change of government has not changed this pattern. Therefore, we urge the Council and its member states to establish a country-specific special repertoire for Sri Lanka and to refer the situation in Sri Lanka to the ICC. We also call on states to condemn the removal of this memorial and to protect Tamil commemorations from intimidation. Justice delayed is justice denied.

Thank you.

Thank you. I give the floor to Center for Gender Justice and Women Empowerment. Not in the room. I give the floor for a joint statement by International Lawyers Org.

We thank the High Commissioner, the ad hoc committee and the group of independent eminent experts for their reports. 25 years after the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, racial discrimination persists across societies, demonstrating the need for the full implementation of its commitments. We agree that education holds transformative potential to address the legacies of colonialism and violence, despite often perpetuating the very inequalities it should dismantle through biased curricula and the erasure of the history and identities of people of African descent, Indigenous peoples, and racial and ethnic minorities. Particularly, young women and girls face compounded forms of intersectional discrimination which substantially undermines the full enjoyment of their human rights and fundamental freedoms. In this perspective, we call upon States to make anti-racism education mandatory at all levels, including historically informed curricula and comprehensive training for educators and public authorities in the prevention and remedy of discrimination. We further stress the importance of Member States effectively addressing racial discrimination and hate speech in virtual spaces through strengthened monitoring, prevention and reporting national mechanisms, with special attention to the protection of youth and children. Ultimately, we urge Member States to recognize the gravity of the these evolving forms of racial discrimination, turn commitments into measurable actions, and fully implement the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. We thank you.
I give the floor now to Action for Development.

Mr. President, we draw the attention of this Council to the human rights violations resulting from the policy of illegal foreigners repatriation plan of Pakistan. The policy has led to the expulsion of over 2.3 million nationals of Afghanistan and represents a breach of the non-refoulement principle. It is in violation of the Convention against Torture, which prohibits the return of individuals to a state where they face a danger of torture, and Article 7 and 9 of ICCPR, regarding arbitrary detention and inhuman treatment. The separation of family with children violate the convention on the rights of child. Afghan refugees holding Afghan citizen card and proof of registration have been expelled without due process. The accelerated campaign of arrest and forced returns of refugees from December to June this year have raised profound concerns and documented by the UN. Women and girls are particularly vulnerable due to restriction on education, employment, and movement. last year, Human Rights Watch has already warned that the renewed deportation campaign exposes Afghan refugees to persecution and severe humanitarian hardship upon their return. On June, the WFP reported that Afghanistan's economy is struggling to absorb millions of such returnees. We urge the Council to ask Pakistan for an immediate halt to the forced returns of Afghan refugees and adopt a national legal framework that codifies the principle of non-refoulement into domestic law.
Thank you. Thank you. I give the floor to Christian Solidarity International.

Christian Solidarity International once again expresses its deep concern over the threats to the survival of the indigenous peoples of West Papua posed by the Indonesian government's military operations and development programs. As of September, the number of internally.

Displaced people in the six provinces of West Papua had risen to 127,000, up from just 105,000 six months ago. CSI's partners on the ground continue to report new arrivals of displaced people in coastal areas.

This displacement is driven by government military operations, which are carried out to protect large-scale mining and farming projects that are driving indigenous Papuans from their lands.

These military operations often claim civilian lives, such as Ilianus Agimbau, a 20-year-old evangelist who was killed in Central Papua province on June 29. CSI echoes the call issued by the Papuan Customary Council on July 1st for the Indonesian government to halt all national strategic projects in the seven customary regions of Papua for independent investigations into serious human rights abuses and for concrete steps towards an end to military operations in West Papua. CSI also supports the call made by several Pacific countries during the last General Assembly for the Indonesian government to facilitate a visit to the region by the High Commissioner for Human Rights.

Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to Association d'Entre Aide Medicale Guinee.

Thank you, Vice President. We note the ever-increasing use of ethnic identity and geographic belonging as a basis for targeting civilians as part of the war in Sudan, which only exacerbates social divisions and fuels hate speech. In various areas, reports have documented the detention of civilians in Darfur by units linked to the Sudanese Armed Forces. Some of them have faced beatings, ill treatment, as well as humiliation on the basis of their identity because they were suspected of aligning with a warring party. In Al-Fasher, at the end of October, we have witnessed murder and abuse of civilians on an ethnic basis. Linking between the ethnic identity and a certain or supposed loyalty to a war and party is something that threatens the principle of non-discrimination. We call upon Sudanese authorities to stop profiling or stereotyping or discriminating against people on the basis of ethnic or geographic identity and to conduct investigations into violations. We call upon this Council to give priority to racism and ethnic discrimination and hate speech in Sudan because dealing with this scourge is a prerequisite for protecting civilians and building peace on the basis of respect for human rights and equality. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I now pass the floor to the Consejero Indigenista Misionario.

The connection of the indigenous people in Brazil and the Indigenous Mission Council is an episode which calls our attention to the grave injustice of the Brazilian justice context. During an official session of the court, it was demonstrated that indigenous people do not have labor rights and that they are involved in conditions similar to slavery. When a system reproduces in an official session racist stereotypes concerning indigenous peoples, the institution itself becomes a space for the reproduction of discrimination. This episode reveals a wider problem. Institutional racism in the justice system doesn't only impact the dignity of indigenous people. We must also establish, or it can also establish barriers to access to justice. thus compromising trust in the judicial institutions across Brazil and undermining the Brazilian constitution. Limited healthcare on the Marshall Islands means cancer patients may need to travel abroad for treatment, separating families, sometimes for extended periods. The harm is also written into the relationship between the people and the land. Many displaced communities have not been able to return to their ancestral atolls, leaving generations disconnected from their land, their culture, and their traditions. In Marshallese custom, women are custodians of the land. Displacement fractures these ties and undermines their authority. Social stigma compounds these harms. Communities are reportedly labeled as "ri bijin," or poison people, with young people experiencing the nuclear legacy as a source of anxiety and internalized shame. The Marshall Islands and diaspora communities require sustained access to healthcare, education, and other social services that can address the impact of the nuclear legacy, including intergenerational trauma and psychosocial harm. Mr. Vice President, Marshallese communities have the right to an effective remedy for the harm caused by the nuclear tests. This includes reparations and guarantees that the harm will not be repeated. However, scarce resources, legal and other barriers mean many are still waiting for this right to be fulfilled. What can justice for the nuclear legacy look like? Well, first, stronger efforts are needed to establish the truth about what happened, who has been affected, and the extent of the harm. To that end, our office recommends that the United States declassify information about the nuclear legacy, including data on radiation exposure and testing records. They will enable the Marshallese to make informed decisions about their health, their land, and their search for justice. Secondly, the damage needs to be repaired. The Compact of Free Association and the Section 177 Agreement on the Settlement of Claims did not cover harm done to future generations, moral damage, environmental degradation, and other forms of harm. These agreements must be interpreted in a manner consistent with the victims' right to an effective remedy. Domestic legal mechanisms in the Marshall Islands have an important role, including traditional rights courts, which has jurisdiction over land and customary law. The Nuclear Claims Tribunal in the Marshall Islands have assessed more than US$2.3 billion in personal injury and property damage claims, yet no claimant has received full compensation due to insufficient funds. We must also acknowledge that repairing damage goes beyond financial compensation. It means addressing the environmental consequences of nuclear testing and ensuring sustained access to social services for affected communities, including the diaspora. And thirdly, justice is about more than claims and courtrooms. The Marshall Islands has identified transitional justice as a means of advancing victims' right to truth, justice, reparation, and guarantees of non-repetition. This approach can draw strength from Marshallese understandings of justice, which emphasizes repairing harm and restoring balance within the community. Accountability is understood as not only being held to account, but as recognizing one's own responsibility. Marshallese students have told my office that justice requires acknowledgment, apology, and action. Affected communities need to be meaningfully involved in every decision concerning them. Women, young people, and others who have traditionally been excluded need to have a central role. Education and outreach about the legacy of nuclear testing can also advance justice by ensuring communities understand what happened and knowing their rights. Mr. Vice President, the Marshallese people did not create this legacy. They should not be left to address it alone. Sustained regional and international support is essential to help the Marshall Islands address the immediate and intergenerational consequences of nuclear testing. It is also vital to advance accountability and justice. During the nuclear tests, the UN Trusteeship Council recommended that precautions be taken against their dangers, but it did not call for an end to the tests. The international community, through the Trusteeship Council, needs to consider steps to acknowledge and apologize for the human rights impact of the nuclear legacy and express solidarity with the victims. Our office is ready to continue providing technical cooperation to the Marshall Islands National Nuclear Commission. Current and future generations of Marshallese need the truth. They need recognition and justice the previous generations have long sought for. Thank you.

Thank you. Now, I give the floor.

To Mr. Bernardo Heine, video message.

Ladies and gentlemen, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this interactive dialogue on the report of the High Commissioner on the challenges and barriers to the full realization of the human rights of the people of the Marshall Islands stemming from the State's nuclear legacy. I support the important recommendations that it contains for the Marshallese's right to justice and accountability, and would like to bring a complementary perspective from my mandate, focusing mainly on how truth and justice, as well as the other transitional justice pillars, relate to and reinforce one another to address this legacy. I have already sent communications last year to both the RMI and the United States in this regard. And I also wish to warmly thank the Marshall Islands and in particular the National Nuclear Commission for their cooperation during my recent travel to the country, during which I notably joined an event at the College of the Marshall Islands. Mr. President, the nuclear tests conducted by the United States between 1946 and 1958 are not just a matter of history. Their consequences are lived every day by the Marshallese communities, in their bodies, in their land, in their ocean, and in their spirit, as Kesi Buki wrote in his famous song, which still resonates over the Pacific. The right to truth, to know what happened, how and why, is crucial for closure as it is for the future. The Marshall Islands stand ready to pursue a truth-seeking process, but full realization of the right to seek and receive information requires access to all records regarding the nuclear legacy, not only about the nuclear blasts themselves, but also about the medical and environmental tests that took place after them. Pursuant to the principle of maximum disclosure, all information held by the US related to the human rights impact of the nuclear testing should therefore be disclosed by default, with national security secrecy being a strictly necessary exception. This right extends beyond access to information and is also essential to the mental and moral integrity of victims and their families. People need to know the extent of the radiation that they have been exposed to, the health risks they continue facing, and the long-term impact of the nuclear tests that they have had on their land and water. For decades, Marshallese peoples were examined, sampled, and studied, and yet they were never given the results of such tests. In the absence of full disclosure, uncertainty and distrust persists, and competing accounts of what happened fill the silence. The humane thing to do is to alleviate this suffering by ensuring full disclosure. Mr. President, Section 177 of the Compact of Free Association that was concluded between the Marshall Islands and the U.S. in 1986 is the agreement that is meant to constitute the full and final settlement of all claims between the RMI and the United States in relation to the nuclear testing program. And under this section, the US accepted responsibility for compensating Marshallese citizens for loss or damage resulting from the nuclear testing. This being said, it was then, and to many extents still is today, impossible to foresee all aspects of human rights violations that flowed from the nuclear testing and the medical experiments that followed, nor to predict the continuous nature of these violations and their transgenerational effects that they This can certainly constitute an important change of circumstance that both the RMI and the US should look into today. In fact, the agreement raises an important questions for victims' right to an effective remedy as well established principles of transitional justice based on international human rights law and international criminal law standards prohibit parties to a transition, whether from an armed conflict to peace, from dictatorship to democracy, or from colonial rule to independence, to bilaterally agree on legal mechanisms that prevent victims to enjoy judicial protection of their rights or to access justice to address gross violations of human rights. Self-adopted or mutually agreed upon amnesties for these violations were unequivocally considered incompatible by international law, as were the adoption of other obstacles such as statutes of limitations or similar procedural hurdles. For Marshallese victims and their families, this is not an abstract question of interstate settlement. It concerns harms that have continued across generations. Mr. President, in addition, measures should be adopted to ensure full reparation. Measures taken so far have proven clearly insufficient. I would reiterate that reparation must not be confused with assistance. as aid and social programs, however valuable, do not specifically recognize victims. Also, measures of restitution should be adopted to clean up and rehabilitate all contaminated communities, as well as psychosocial rehabilitation for moral harm of exposure, displacement, and decades of uncertainty, which have never been addressed or treated. Also, apologies from the US and UN authorities are yet to be formulated. Preserving historical truth and memory is also essential, especially in resisting efforts to deny or revise this history. The creation of museums, exhibits, and memorials are urgently necessary, in my view, while survivors are still here to share their stories. Mr. President, The challenge is also today about preventing further harm, including regarding public health. A national program for screening cancer and providing early treatment would not only be a form of reparation, but would be mostly a prevention, and it would save lives. The environmental risks are equally pressing, in particular on Inuvik, where the ruined dome where radioactive waste has been held, risks leaking, in particular considering rising seas. With climate change, the dome presents renewed immense risks to the Marshall Islands and indeed to the entire planet as it constitutes a nuclear ticking bomb in the Pacific. The international community should urgently support the RMI to scientifically assess the risks and adopt concrete measures to prevent additional damage. Without urgent action, the harm of the past will become the harm of the future. Excellencies, I should finish by thanking the Rhamajilin who welcomed me on their atolls, in particular Alsen Kelen, a Bikini elder with whom I went to Kili and Ejet, where most displaced Bikinians are. Alson went back to live on his home island after the American president's declaration that it was safe to do so, and he lived there four years before being told again to leave as the impact of the radiations were still too dangerous for humans to bear. And while the Department of Energy has tested the soil, the water, the fish, the coconuts, and the vegetable plantations that it has kept on Bikini since, it never did early cancer screening on Alson sitting before you today. nor on any other Marshall Islands for that matter. And let's take a second to let this sink in. Think of what this means and realize that this tragedy is a human tragedy. Mr. President, technical assistance to the National Nuclear Commission is needed, including concrete transfer of knowledge and resources. And I call on the High Commissioner to ensure that from the perspective of their respective mandate, the IAEA, the WHO, the UNFPA, UNESCO, UNDP, IOM, UNICEF, and others are involved in, work together and contribute to addressing the country's nuclear legacy. About 80 years ago, when the Marshall Islands were placed under trusteeship, the international community and the United States made a promise to protect the Marshallese people, who have waited with extraordinary dignity for the world to keep its word. And it's now the responsibility of the international community to do good on its promise. Kamau Tata, thank you, Mr. President.
Muchas gracias. Thank you very much. I'm now going to pass the floor to Mr. Alston Cullen for his presentation.

Mr. President, Deputy High Commissioners, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is an honor to join you today. For me, the nuclear legacy is not history. It is the story of my life. Today, I serve as a commissioner for the Marshall Island National Nuclear Commission, carrying not only the responsibility of that position, but also the lived experience of a people who for 80 years have carried a loss that is hard to put into words. My earliest memories of Happy days as a young boy living and thriving in Bikini, unaware of the invisible threat present in the environment around us. I remember my grandparents and the men and women of the community going about the ordinary rhythm of island life. Men shaping wood and working on canoes beneath the trees, women weaving, preparing food, caring for our families, and caring for their knowledge through the everyday work of the community. At the time, none of this seemed remarkable to me. I did not know to call it traditional knowledge. It was simply how we lived. I assumed these were things I would always see and learn naturally as I grew older. I could not live, I could not have known then that this ordinary way of life would be interrupted, or that the knowledge I absorbed simply by growing up around my elders would one day be threatened. Only much later I understand that some of the everyday chores were only becoming memories, and that keeping them alive would one day require a certain level of effort and commitment. In our language, means storytelling, but it is more than simply telling event in order. It is how we pass down memory. It is how we teach our children who they are and how things work. It is how we carry truth from generation to the next. And in term of the nuclear legacy, this is webinar or story is a quiet memory that wasn't spoken of at home and in school. It was, if we had become preoccupied with surviving the new way of life of displacement and uncertainty without fully realizing it, the life we once knew quietly slip away. The changes did we not happen to at all once. Families adjusted to new islands, new communities. We grew up away from the island my parents and our grandparents called home. And we, each generation, adapted to the circumstances before them. Some of the knowledge that connected us to our land, our ocean, and one another became one more difficult to carry forward. This became much clearer to us through the work of the National Nuclear Commission. Shortly after the establishment, one of the first priority we simply had to do is to listen. It also means strengthening our own national capacity to understand and respond to these consequences. 80 years on, History has been documented, consultation held, report have been written, resolution adopted, recommendation put forward. This important work has brought us to a point where we must now be built up this foundation with greater urgency and resolve. Mr. President, that will we have, what will we have leave the next generation the lessons of this history, our unsolved legacy. For more than 70 years, our people have come to these halls seeking recognition, justice, and meaningful resolution to the nuclear legacy. That appeal has already passed from one generation to the next. My grandchildren should not have returned to these same halls years from now to continue a chant that has echoed here for generations. Let this be the generation that turns decades of testimony, evidence, and promises into action and leave our children a different legacy.
Thank you very much. It's now my pleasure to pass the floor to Ms. Alice Ward for her presentation.

Mr. President, Deputy, High Commissioner, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I have the privilege and honor to speak before you today on behalf of the diaspora youth and as a daughter and granddaughter of Buguni. In middle school, sitting in my social studies class, on the board was written the Pacific Islands. As a young Marshallese girl, I was ecstatic. I thought that I would finally be able to learn more about my island and my fellow classmates would be able to learn the history of my people as well. Unfortunately, that excitement came to an end quickly. But when the topic got to the Marshall Islands, the only information that was given was that the Marshall Islands was a country in poverty. My teacher did not teach about the rich culture, the community, or the deep history. Neither did she speak of the violence of 67 nuclear weapons that devastated my country. Confused, I raised my hand and asked my teacher about the nuclear testing that was done in the Marshall Islands. She had no idea what I was speaking about and insisted that she was merely going based off of what was in the school curriculum. I must admit that I had a very difficult time preparing my statement today because there's so much pressure in knowing things and it is in that uncertainty that creates more questions. How do I explain something that I don't know? How do I describe what has not been yet declassified? How do I paint a picture for a moment which, though I've never seen it, I continue to feel? I was born and raised in the United States. I did not grow up in the Marshall Islands. However, despite the distance, I never felt completely separated from my identity because our community found ways to create home wherever we were. Although my family had a whole life established in the United States, I always knew I belonged to the Marshall Islands. Before I was born, my family moved to the United States to look for better healthcare and a better education. Due to the language barriers, they had to work harder than the average American just to provide and make ends meet. Growing up was difficult, wanting to stay connected to my roots, but also wanting to fit in with my friends. Not completely fitting into either group, being too Americanized for the Marshallese, but then being too different for the Americans. The only way I ever felt connected was being close to family, going to church, and staying involved in the community. Although it is a small struggle, its effects impact us immensely. The difficulty of connecting across cultures can actually make those relationships more meaningful because they require patience, openness, and a genuine effort to understand one another. Being Marshallese has taught me that my culture is something I should be proud to share, rather than something I feel pressured to hide or simplify for other people. Why does this burden fall on me, on someone who wasn't even there during the tests yet, 80 years later, continues to bear the weight of a legacy no Marshallese then or now ever asked for? Today, I am not just here to speak about the hardship that we've endured. I am here hopeful for a better tomorrow. I realize that not knowing every part of history does not separate me from it. Instead, it gives me a reason to learn, to ask questions, and to listen more carefully to those who came before me. The disconnect has encouraged me to ask more questions, not only about the nuclear weapons testing program, displacement, loss of traditional knowledge, but about home. Our elders carry stories about what happened to our islands, our land, and our communities because of nuclear testing. We understand the importance of learning from those who came before us, and I believe it is our responsibility as youth to pass that knowledge on to the next generation. I realize now that reconnecting with my identity can begin with something as simple as learning to weave the pieces together. Initially, the strands can seem tangled and it's difficult to understand how they will ever come together. And perhaps I don't need to understand everything at once. I can begin with one strand at a time, one story, one conversation, one lesson. and trust that with each one, I am coming closer to understanding who I am and what I will carry forward. But I shouldn't have to do this alone. The Marshallese people shouldn't have to face the nuclear justice alone. We need access to the truth about what happened to our people and our islands. We need our history to be recognized and taught so that the next Marshallese child sitting in a classroom does not have to explain her own history to her teacher. or to pour their heart out in a room full of strangers in Geneva, calling for things to change. Young Marshallese in our islands and throughout the diaspora also have a place in deciding what justice looks like. I may not have witnessed the nuclear test, yet I inherited their legacy. But I also inherited the responsibility and the hope to help share, to help shape what comes next. As I close, I would also like to recognize the touch of pink you see among our delegation today. As we begin Breast Cancer Awareness Month, we wear pink in honor of those who have faced breast cancer, those we have lost, and the families who have stood beside them. With this spirit of strength and unity, I thank you for the opportunity to be here today.
Thank you very much. I'd now like to recognize Mr. Sheldon Ricklin for his presentation.

Mr. President, Deputy High Commissioner, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I'm very honored here to be here with you today. I'm here as a Marshallese family doctor who has worked in the Marshall Islands and currently works closely with the large diaspora community in the state of Arkansas. During my time in the Marshall Islands, I chaired the National Medical Referral Committee and was the Director of Clinical Operations for the U.S. Department of Energy's Special Medical Care Program. It was during my tenure in these capacities that I became very familiar with many cases that came before the committee to be referred out of the country for medical services not available locally. Many of these cases were of patients with cancers, requiring either definitive diagnosis or treatment that could not be provided on island. In the Marshall Islands, one of the criteria for denial of a patient's referral is if the patient's cancer diagnosis has a five-year survival rate of less than 50%. Unfortunately, the medical referral committee had to deny several cases for this reason. Many of the patients denied, we knew personally and professionally. Being a physician does not separate our personal or family relations from the people we are serving. Some of the cases were of young Marshallese patients or patients with families of their own who had advanced cancer. This was part of the work that we did not enjoy nor took pride in, especially when members of the community characterized it as "playing God." Over the years, it took its toll on us, but we persevered because we had to. The Marshall Islands has high cancer rates that affects both sexes with more propensity to the female sex, people from all age groups, including young mothers with young children. I can personally attest today that it does. I have seen it and continue to see it in my current medical practice in Arkansas. Current reports reveal that there are now more Marshallese living outside than in the Marshall Islands. We leave our beautiful islands in the blue Pacific to the continental U.S., seeking a better life for ourselves and our children and grandchildren. We seek educational and employment opportunities and better healthcare. We know that the United States has more advanced medical technology and expertise. We see the United States as our big brother. We have a long, deep-rooted shared history, including our nuclear legacy. Our children enlist in the U.S. military to serve alongside their brothers and sisters in efforts to keep world peace. The rate of enlistment from our Micronesian region is higher per capita than any one U.S. state. We expect to be treated as family as we treat them as family. We expect to have access to comprehensive first-rate healthcare when we move to the U.S. Sadly, we do not. As a doctor at a federally qualified health center in Northwest Arkansas, majority of my patients are Marshallese. I am blessed to be their primary care physician because working with them makes me feel like I'm working back home in the islands. I feel that community connectedness, that family closeness. Each patient is a family member. I treat them as family in a culturally sensitive approach. When they are admitted or die from their conditions, I feel the pain because they are family. I attend their funerals, too many to count, to or to drink from the cup that is filled with sour liquid. That's our cultural expression, that we will be there together for each other, especially during just such hard and heavy times. That's the Remajel way, the Marshallese way. It is said that medical care accounts for only 20% of a person's overall health outcomes, while the remaining 80% are driven by social, environmental, and behavioral factors. That means that I can give them my 100% of my medical expertise, but if I do not address their health insurance, housing, school, food, and family needs, I am only providing them with 20% of what they need, only 20%. That is the reason I'm a community advocate. I want to make a difference for my family, my people, including those in the diaspora. That is why I am in this space today. Life in the U.S. is not easy. One must put in the work to learn how to live comfortably in a place that's not ours. We have to understand the complicated healthcare system that's very different from ours and is not very user-friendly, especially in terms of language access. But we sacrifice for our families. we leave the islands to find another home for potential brighter future for our families. In 2024, Her Excellency Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine declared a national health emergency regarding non-communicable diseases or NCDs, including cardiovascular and respiratory conditions, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, and cancers, among others. These account for more than 80% of the premature deaths in the islands. Besides cancer, I believe that all the other conditions are also related to our nuclear legacy. give you uproot a culture who is dependent on getting fresh, healthy seafood from the rich Pacific waters on a daily basis, who grow and harvest local fruits and vegetables regularly, and replace it with a culture that eats imported, quote unquote, safer, unradiated canned foods that are high in salt, saturated fats, and preservatives, you will have a population with high rates of NCDs. As a Marshallese doctor working with the diaspora, the demographics and conditions I see in my patient population are the same as those back home, same chronic diseases and cancer conditions. The nuclear legacy, now 80 years old, has extended beyond the shores of the Marshall Islands. It lives and will continue to expand in the diaspora communities outside the islands, It is my hope today that we go beyond dialogue and we do meaningful, tangible health outcome measures for our Marshallese people wherever they are. They have sacrificed enough for the good of mankind. Thank you. Thank you very much.

Mr. Vice President, we welcome the High Commissioner's report and this dialogue. We also thank the panelists for their important contributions. Indeed, the report considers how justice as a pillar of transitional justice applies to our nuclear legacy. This is an important question that we in the Marshall Islands have grappled with for too long. How can we have justice when we are told by those responsible that the matter is settled and that is final? Between 1946 and 1958, while under the UN trusteeship, the United States of America conducted 67 known nuclear weapon tests in our islands. When our people petitioned for this to stop, the UN Trusteeship Council issued resolutions that allowed it to continue. The report recommends that the UN Trusteeship Council acknowledge and apologize for this. The previous report included a recommendation that the United States of America also acknowledge and apologize for the human rights impacts of the nuclear legacy. Indeed, an apology would be an important step towards justice for the victims and survivors of this legacy. The UN stood as our islands were bombed, our human rights were violated, and our people were experimented on under Project 4.1 without their consent. In February of this year, at the 61st session Our president, Dr. Hilda Hiene, described this legacy as a monumental failure of multilateralism. Because of this failure, the people of Pikini and Rongelap remain displaced, longing to return to their ancestral lands. On Eniwetok, people are living in a nuclear waste dump concealed under a massive concrete dome. This is their home, and that toxic dump is called their pillow. My own people from Ailuk are often ignored in this legacy. Despite being exposed to radioactive fallout, they were not evacuated, and we have suffered hardships to this day. Truth be told, the entirety of the Marshall Islands is affected. These are the consequences of the UN trusteeship that failed our people, under which we are misled, exploited, and to this day, denied the acknowledgment, truth, and justice that we deserve. If this legacy is left unaddressed, the UN will continue to fail the people of the Marshall Islands. The harm is not only historical. We live through it today, and the continued denial of an effective remedy has forced us to come before this Council to ask for help. Mr. Vice-President, the report is clear. There has not yet been a comprehensive and just settlement of the claims that arise from the nuclear testing program. Without truth, there can be no justice. But justice, as we understand it, is not vengeance. Our people's earliest petitions to the UN were not made in reputation of the United States of America, but for the well-being of our people. What we have always asked for is, which means what is correct. And as the report reminds us, for forgiveness to be granted, It must be first sought. In the Marshall Islands, when speaking of reconciliation, we also speak of, which means cleansing. Cleansing does not mean forgive and forget. In 2024, at the 57th session, President Haini called for a meaningful reconciliation and honesty to finally deal with the past, to come to terms with uncomfortable truth, to devise solutions, and to move forward together. We need honesty and full truth. We need our environment restored and our people returned to good health. And we need accountability for the human rights, environmental, health consequences of the nuclear legacy. This year marks 80 years of this nuclear legacy in the Marshall Islands, a legacy that is not known for -- a legacy that is not of our own making, a legacy we never wanted, A legacy we are forced to endure and survive. 80 years on, our people are still here, still asking for what is correct,, still asking for nuclear legacy to be cleansed,. Hear our stories, take them to heart, acknowledge the facts, and work with us to ensure a better future for our children. We count on the Council's continued support and ask for all States to stand in solidarity with the Marshall Islands in our efforts to ensure our future of our people free of the human rights challenges that we have endured over the last 80 years due to the nuclear legacy. Thank you, and komo lauda, Mr. Vice-President.
